## Introduction

The human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a neglected oncogenic retrovirus that primarily affects marginalized and isolated populations. After several decades of chronic infection, the virus is directly responsible for an aggressive form of T-cell lymphoma (ATLL, Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma) and several autoimmune disorders, particularly HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP). Moreover, even seemingly asymptomatic carriers (ACs) face a significantly higher risk of death from indirect complications. @schierhout2020 @valcarcel2022 Although transmission has been controlled in some developed regions, HTLV-1 remains disattended across most of the global south. @nishijima2019 @martin2018 On top of that, HTLV-1 predominantly impacts rural populations with low genetic admixture and limited healthcare access. @vantienen2012 @djuicy2018 @einsiedel2021

Efforts to identify high-risk ACs have centered on three key determinants: viral, host, and environmental factors. Among viral factors, the current HTLV-1 classification (e.g., Cosmopolitan \[a–d\], Japanese, West African) is based on LTR and env region diversity, which aligns with geographic distribution but lacks clear ties to disease outcomes. Functional genomic differences seems more pronounced in the Tax protein, with Tax A (Transcontinental) trending to worse survival among ATLL cases. @sakihama2017 Clinically, proviral load and oligoclonality remain the most widely adopted prognostic markers, while emerging evidence suggests defective proviruses may contribute to immune evasion in ATLL progression. @katsuya2019 @estrada-grossmann2025 However, most findings have been validated primarily in Japanese cohorts, limiting their generalizability.

Host factors are mainly attributed to immune diversity where HLA seems to play a central role in why less than 10% developed ATLL or HAM/TSP. The infection seems to have predomunance for specific ethnicties, and intrafamilial predisposition. The divergence confers any deleterious effect remains unclear, Research gaps persist in understanding genetic susceptibility.some HLA has been demostrated to be protective family history of ATL. @iwanaga2010

Enviromental factors, such as Strongyloides coinfection have been previously linked to ATLL progression, however its mechanisms remain not elucidated. Considering that HTLV-1 is clearly endemic in south America. Comprehensive evaluation of HTLV-1 infected population remain scarce. risk factors for latino population is still scarcing. Peru has a particular interest because it has reported the highest incidence of ATL from the region and is characterized by its high indigenous component from all south american countires. We aimed to evaluate the explore virology, immune and host diversity of HTLV-1 infection using a highthrough output aproach in South America.

## Methods

### Population study and HTLV-1 confirmation

After informed consent, blood samples were collected from patients of the prospective HTLV-1 cohort at the Instituto de Medicina Tropical Alexander Von Humbold (Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, Lima-Peru). The study was approved by the Ethics committee of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, Miayazaki University and Kagoshima University. All patients were previously HTLV-1 screened and confirmed by an Enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay (ELISA), and PCR-based approach locally. DNA extraction

### Methods

Recombination analyses

Recombination was initially evaluated using the phi-test followed by a exploratory screening using RDP, GENECONV, Bootscan, MaxChi, SisCan and 3Seq and LARD, implemented in RDP4.5. Potential recombination was suspected when at least four methods showed a Bonferroni-corrected P-value threshold of 0.05(or smaller). Sequences with potential recombination signal were evaluated with GARD, implemented in Hyphy, and excluded from the final data set. An exploratory screening for recombination was performed using phylogenetic methods (Bootscan and RDP), and nucleotide substitution methods (Chimaera, GENECONV, MaxChi, SisCan and 3Seq), Additionally phi-test performed in the RDP4.5 software. Sequences with potential recombination signal were considered when at least four alogorithms reached a threshold p-value of 0.05 with Bonferroni correction. GARD implemented in Hyphy was used to evaluate

Following reads extraction from the chromosome 6, coverage and quality score analyses were performed for all HLA regions. High-resolution HLA typing was carried out using OptiType (2-field resolution for HLA-I) and HLA-LA (3-field resolution for HLA-I/II). Allotypes failing quality thresholds (score \<0.8 or average coverage \<20) were discarded. Results from both bioinformatics tools were pairwise compared, and considering the average coverage for HLA-II, only HLA-I was considered to further analysis. The concordances and Cohen's Kappa between HLA-LA and Optitype were 93%, 85%, and 100% for HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C, respectively. The HLA-LA pipeline was selected for further analyses.Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) was tested for each locus using the exact test implemented on the pegas package with 1000 replicates with a significance threshold of α=0.05. Pairwise F<sub>ST</sub> was estimated using Weir & Cockerham’s (1984) method with 10,000 bootstrap replicates implemented on the package hierfstat. Significant differentiation was inferred when 95% CIs excluded zero.

HLA class I allele frequencies were calculated after reduction to 2-field resolution using the *reduceHlaCalls* function from the package midasHLA. Frequencies for the Peruvian population were obtained using the function *getHlaFrequencies* and compared to the USA National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP) populations that were retrieved from Allele Frequency Net Database (http://www.allelefrequencies.net/).

# Results

A total of 67 patients with confirmed HTLV-1 infection were included in the study, comprising 10 HAM/TSP patients and 57 asymptomatic carriers (ACs). The lifetime *Strongyloides* infection rate was 56.7% overall and more frequent among males. No association was found between *Strongyloides* infection and HTLV-1-related complications. Demographic and epidemiological characteristics are detailed in **Table 1**. During the 5-year follow-up, the progression rate to ATL among ACs was 5.3% (3 cases). Notably, the 5-year mortality rate was 15%, although 12% of patients were lost to follow-up during COVID-19 pandemic.

A total of 71 DNA samples—corresponding to 67 patients (including 4 serial samples)—were analyzed. The median HTLV-1 genome coverage in the Peruvian cohort was 158X (IQR: 23-218); (**Supplementary Figure 1**). After excluding 4 samples with less than 5x coverage, the final dataset comprised 63 cases (**Supplementary Figure 2**). Among these, 3 cases (4.8%) harbored type II defective viruses (5’LTR-deleted; **Figure 1A**). Notably, 2 out of 3 ATL cases and 1 AC exhibited these deletions. No type I defective viruses were detected in this cohort.

HLA-I allele frequencies

The Peruvian HTLV-1 cohort exhibited distinct HLA-I allele distributions, with A*02:01 being the most frequent allele at the HLA-A locus (44%), followed by A*24:02 (17%) and A*68:01 (7%). The HLA-B locus showed equal frequencies for B*35:01 and B*35:05 (12% each), with B*48:01 at 11%, while the HLA-C locus was dominated by C*04:01 (29%), followed by C*01:02 (18%) and C\*07:02 (13%). Comparative analyses with the NMDP database and a Japanese HTLV-1 cohort revealed population-specific variations, with HLA-A and HLA-C conforming to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p=0.06 and p=0.33, respectively), but HLA-B showing significant deviation (p=0.01), likely reflecting its well-documented role in balancing selection or cohort-specific demographic factors. Complete allele frequencies are detailed in Supplementary Table 1. The Peruvian and Japanese cohorts showed significant moderate genetic differentiation (mean F<sub>ST</sub> = 0.047, 95% CI \[0.023, 0.072\]), consistent with population-specific HLA allele frequency distributions.
